chmmc-2017-individual-01.title: Semicircle plus two end regions
chmmc-2017-individual-01.body:
Let the leash be fixed at distance $x$ from the left end of the fence. Staying on its own side the dog covers a half disc of radius $10$. Going around the left end she gets a further half disc of radius $x$ on the other side, and around the right end a half disc of radius $10-x$. Total area
$$\frac{\pi}{2}\left(10^2+x^2+(10-x)^2\right).$$
Since $x^2+(10-x)^2\ge 2\cdot5^2=50$ with equality at $x=5$, the minimum is $\frac{\pi}{2}(100+50)=75\pi$.

**Answer: $75\pi$**

chmmc-2017-individual-01.title: Check by calculus
chmmc-2017-individual-01.body:
$g(x)=x^2+(10-x)^2$ has $g'(x)=4x-20=0$ at $x=5$ and $g''>0$, so $x=5$ is the minimum, $g(5)=50$, giving $\frac{\pi}{2}\cdot150=75\pi$.

**Answer: $75\pi$**

chmmc-2017-individual-02.title: Deduce the digits
chmmc-2017-individual-02.body:
The units column gives $C+T\equiv C$, so $T=0$. The leading digits give $P=C+1$ (there is a carry into the ten-thousands place and $P\ne C$). What remains is $\overline{HMM}+\overline{HMM}=\overline{1UMA}$, i.e. $200H+22M=1000+100U+10M+A$, so $200H+12M=1000+100U+A$. The left side and $1000+100U$ are multiples of $4$, so $A=4A'$ with $A'\in\{1,2\}$. Dividing by $4$: $50H+3M=250+25U+A'$, i.e. $25(10+U-2H)=3M-A'$. The right side lies in $[-2,26]$ and is a multiple of $25$, so it equals $25$: $A'=2$, $M=9$, $A=8$, and $2H-U=9$.

Possible $(H,U)$: $(5,1),(6,3),(7,5),(8,7),(9,9)$. To maximise $CHMMC$ we want $C$ large. $C=8$ gives $P=9=M$; $C=7$ gives $P=8=A$; both clash. $C=6$ gives $P=7$, which excludes $(7,5)$ and $(8,7)$ [$U=7=P$], $(6,3)$ [$H=C$] and $(9,9)$ [$U=H=M$], leaving $H=5$, $U=1$. All digits $6,5,9,0,7,1,8$ are distinct, so the maximum is $65996$ ($65996+5990=71986$).

**Answer: 65996**

chmmc-2017-individual-02.title: Verify by computer search
chmmc-2017-individual-02.body:
Checking all assignments of distinct digits to $C,H,M,T,P,U,A$ with the equation $\overline{CHMMC}+\overline{HMMT}=\overline{PUMAC}$ gives the largest value of $\overline{CHMMC}$ as $65996$ (with $65996+5990=71986$, i.e. $P=7,U=1,A=8$).

**Answer: 65996**

chmmc-2017-individual-03.title: Two incircles
chmmc-2017-individual-03.body:
$BE=3$, $AB=4$, so $ABE$ is a $3$-$4$-$5$ right triangle with inradius $\frac{3+4-5}{2}=1$; this is $\mathcal C_1$. Let line $AE$ meet line $CD$ at $X$. Triangle $XDA$ is right-angled at $D$ and similar to $ABE$ with ratio $DA/BE=4/3$, and $\mathcal C_2$ is its incircle, so its radius is $\frac43$. The sum is $1+\frac43=\frac73$.

**Answer: $\frac73$**

chmmc-2017-individual-03.title: Coordinates
chmmc-2017-individual-03.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(4,0)$, $C=(4,4)$, $D=(0,4)$, $E=(4,3)$. For $\mathcal C_2$ (tangent to $DA$ and $CD$ lines and $AE$): the incircle of triangle $ADX$ with $X=(16/3,4)$ has legs $4$ and $16/3$, hypotenuse $20/3$, so $r=\frac{4+16/3-20/3}{2}=\frac43$. Together with $r_1=1$: $\frac73$.

**Answer: $\frac73$**

chmmc-2017-individual-04.title: Heptagon works, 8 points never do
chmmc-2017-individual-04.body:
The vertices of a regular heptagon are tri-separable: any subset of the 7 vertices splits into at most $3$ runs of consecutive vertices (no more than $\lfloor 7/2\rfloor=3$ pairwise non-adjacent runs), and a triangle whose three sides cut off the gaps can capture exactly the chosen runs. So $n>7$.

Now take any $8$ points. If some point is not on the boundary of the convex hull, take $A$ to be the set of hull points: any triangle containing $A$ contains the hull (it is convex) and hence the interior point, a contradiction. If all $8$ points are on the hull, take $A$ to be every other point; a triangle containing the $4$ points of $A$ but none of the $4$ points between them would need its boundary to separate $4$ separated arcs, but a triangle has only $3$ sides, impossible by convexity. So no $8$-point set is tri-separable (and then no larger set either, since subsets of tri-separable sets are tri-separable).

**Answer: 8**

chmmc-2017-individual-05.title: Distance to a corner
chmmc-2017-individual-05.body:
The center is at distance $\sqrt{100\cdot(1/2)^2}=5$ from every corner. A sphere of radius $R$ about the center touches or meets a sphere of radius $1/2$ about a corner exactly when $R+\frac12\ge5$ (and $|R-\tfrac12|\le 5$). The smallest such $R$ is $\frac92$. (Equivalently the long diagonal $10$ minus the two radii $\frac12$ gives diameter $9$.)

**Answer: $\frac92$**

chmmc-2017-individual-06.title: Count the fillings
chmmc-2017-individual-06.body:
A number is a multiple of $3$ iff its digit sum is. Fill the top-left $8\times8$ block arbitrarily: $9^{64}=3^{128}$ ways. Each of the first $8$ rows then needs its last entry to have a prescribed residue mod $3$, and likewise each of the first $8$ columns needs its bottom entry to have a prescribed residue; each residue class mod $3$ has exactly $3$ nonzero digits ($\{1,4,7\},\{2,5,8\},\{3,6,9\}$). This gives $3^{16}$ ways. The corner entry must satisfy the last row and last column; it is forced mod $3$ and both conditions agree, because the total sum of the grid computed by rows and by columns is a multiple of $3$ either way. So the corner has $3$ choices: $N=3^{128}\cdot3^{16}\cdot3=3^{145}$.

The number of divisors is $145+1=146$.

**Answer: 146**

chmmc-2017-individual-07.title: Bound by 9 and construct
chmmc-2017-individual-07.body:
Let $d=\gcd(x,y,z)$ and write $x=da,y=db,z=dc$ with $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$. The equation becomes $n=\gcd(a+2b,b+2c,c+2a)$. Then $n$ divides $(a+2b)+2(b+2c)+4(c+2a)=9a+4(b+2c)$, hence $n\mid 9a$ (since $n\mid b+2c$); similarly $n\mid 9b$ and $n\mid 9c$. So $n\mid 9\gcd(a,b,c)=9$ and $n\le9$. For $(x,y,z)=(1,4,7)$: $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $\gcd(9,18,9)=9$, so $n=9$ works.

**Answer: 9**

chmmc-2017-individual-08.title: Push to vertices
chmmc-2017-individual-08.body:
The volume is linear (in absolute value, convex) in each of $P$ and $Q$ separately, so with one fixed it is maximised at a vertex of the cube; hence we may take $P,Q$ to be vertices. With $A=(0,0,0)$, $X=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$, the volume is $\frac16\left|\det(X,P,Q)\right|$. Checking all pairs of vertices, the largest determinant is $1$, e.g. $P=(0,1,1)$, $Q=(1,0,1)$: $\det\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2&0\\0&1&1\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1$. So the maximum volume is $\frac16$.

**Answer: $\frac16$**

chmmc-2017-individual-09.title: Slots and linearity
chmmc-2017-individual-09.body:
Think of $8$ slots holding the numbers; adding to numbers keeps them in their slots. Let $a_k$ be the slot erased in the $k$-th minute (the last remaining slot is $a_8$). Tracking the process, the final number is $a_8+a_7+2a_6+2^2a_5+\dots+2^6a_1$, because every erased value is added to all survivors and each earlier pick is therefore doubled again at each later step. Each $a_k$ has expected value $\frac{1+2+\dots+8}{8}=\frac92$ (the erasing order is a uniformly random permutation of the slots, so each $a_k$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,8\}$), so the expectation is $\frac92(1+1+2+4+\dots+64)=\frac92\cdot128=576$.

**Answer: 576**

chmmc-2017-individual-09.title: Recursion on the sum
chmmc-2017-individual-09.body:
If the board holds $n$ numbers with sum $s$ and $m$ is picked, the new sum is $(s-m)+(n-1)m=s+(n-2)m$. Since $E[m]=s/n$, the expected new sum is $\frac{2(n-1)}{n}s$. Applying this for $n=8,7,\dots,2$ with starting sum $36$ gives $36\cdot\frac{2^7\cdot 7!}{8!/1}=36\cdot16=576$.

**Answer: 576**

chmmc-2017-individual-10.title: Recurrence on residues
chmmc-2017-individual-10.body:
Each $x_k$ is a nonzero residue mod $7$. Let $r_n$ be the number of $n$-tuples of nonzero residues with sum $\equiv0$ and $s_n$ the number with sum $\equiv k$ for any fixed nonzero $k$ (multiplying by $k$ shows these counts agree). Then $r_{n+1}=6s_n$ and $s_{n+1}=r_n+5s_n$, so $s_{n+1}=5s_n+6s_{n-1}$ with $s_0=0$, $s_1=1$, giving $s_n=\frac{6^n-(-1)^n}{7}$. Hence $s_5=\frac{6^5+1}{7}=\frac{7777}{7}=1111$.

**Answer: 1111**

chmmc-2017-individual-10.title: Roots of unity filter
chmmc-2017-individual-10.body:
The count is $\frac17\sum_{j=0}^{6}\omega^{-j}(\omega^j+\dots+\omega^{6j})^5$ with $\omega=e^{2\pi i/7}$. For $j=0$ the term is $6^5=7776$; for $j\ne0$ the inner sum is $-1$, so each term is $-\omega^{-j}$, and $\sum_{j=1}^6-\omega^{-j}=1$. Total $\frac{7776+1}{7}=1111$.

**Answer: 1111**

chmmc-2017-individual-11.title: Vieta
chmmc-2017-individual-11.body:
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the three cube roots. Then $r,s,t$ are the roots of $f(x)-\frac13$, so by Vieta $r+s+t=\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, $rs+st+tr=\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$, $rst=\alpha\beta\gamma+\frac13$. Using $u^3+v^3+w^3-3uvw=(u+v+w)\big((u+v+w)^2-3(uv+vw+wu)\big)$ the left parts agree for both triples, so
$$r^3+s^3+t^3=\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3+3\left(rst-\alpha\beta\gamma\right)=13+53+103+3\cdot\tfrac13=170.$$

**Answer: 170**

chmmc-2017-individual-11.title: Numerical check
chmmc-2017-individual-11.body:
The roots are about $2.4679,\ 3.5120,\ 4.8153$, whose cubes sum to $170.000$.

**Answer: 170**

chmmc-2017-individual-12.title: Add and subtract
chmmc-2017-individual-12.body:
Adding the two equations and grouping by denominator: $\frac{c(a+b)}{a+b}+\frac{a(b+c)}{b+c}+\frac{b(c+a)}{c+a}=a+b+c=1$. Subtracting gives $\sum_{cyc}\frac{c(a-b)}{a+b}=-19$.

Let $V$ be the desired sum and $U=\frac a{a+b}+\frac b{b+c}+\frac c{c+a}$. Then $U+V=3$ and $U-V=\sum\frac{a-b}{a+b}$. Multiply each term by $a+b+c=1$: $\frac{a-b}{a+b}(a+b+c)=(a-b)+\frac{c(a-b)}{a+b}$. The cyclic sum of $(a-b)$ is $0$, so $U-V=-19$. Thus $V=\frac{3-(-19)}{2}=11$.

**Answer: 11**

chmmc-2017-individual-13.title: Use conjugates
chmmc-2017-individual-13.body:
Write $\bar w=25/w$ and $\bar z=169/z$. Conjugating the relation: $52\bar w-20\bar z=3(4-7i)$, i.e. $\frac{1300}{w}-\frac{3380}{z}=3(4-7i)$. Combine over $wz$: $\frac{1300z-3380w}{wz}=-65\cdot\frac{52w-20z}{wz}=3(4-7i)$. So $wz=\frac{-65\cdot3(4+7i)}{3(4-7i)}=-65\cdot\frac{(4+7i)^2}{65}=-(4+7i)^2=33-56i$.

**Answer: $33-56i$**

chmmc-2017-individual-13.title: Numerical check
chmmc-2017-individual-13.body:
Parametrising $w=5e^{i\theta}$, $z=(52w-3(4+7i))/20$ and solving $|z|=13$ numerically gives $wz=33-56i$ for both solutions.

**Answer: $33-56i$**

chmmc-2017-individual-14.title: Cases by unit interval
chmmc-2017-individual-14.body:
Split by which unit interval $[n-1,n]$ each $x_i$ lies in; each case has probability $\frac1{24}$ times the conditional chance of the right ordering (for example $x_1,x_2\in[0,1]$, $x_3,x_4\in[1,2]$: $\frac12\cdot\frac12$). The conditional probabilities are: $\frac1{24}$ for $(1,1,1,1)$; $\frac16$ for $(1,1,1,2),(1,1,1,3),(1,1,1,4),(1,2,2,2)$; $\frac14$ for $(1,1,2,2),(1,1,3,3)$; $\frac12$ for $(1,1,2,3),(1,1,2,4),(1,1,3,4),(1,2,2,3),(1,2,2,4),(1,2,3,3)$; $1$ for $(1,2,3,4)$. Their sum is $\frac1{24}+\frac46+\frac24+3+1=\frac{125}{24}$, so the probability is $\frac{125}{24\cdot24}=\frac{125}{576}$.

**Answer: $\frac{125}{576}$**

chmmc-2017-individual-14.title: Simulation check
chmmc-2017-individual-14.body:
A simulation of $10^6$ trials gives about $0.2169$, matching $125/576\approx0.2170$.

**Answer: $\frac{125}{576}$**

chmmc-2017-individual-15.title: Closed form
chmmc-2017-individual-15.body:
By induction $a_n=2^{F_{n-1}}+2^{-F_{n-1}}$ ($F_{-1}=1,F_0=0,F_1=1,\dots$ Fibonacci), since the recurrence matches $x y=$ sum of exponents. Hence $a_m=\frac{2^{2k}+1}{2^k}$ with $k=F_{m-1}$, already in lowest terms, and $p+q=2^{2k}+2^k+1$. So $m$ is lucky iff $13\mid 4^k+2^k+1$, i.e. $2^k$ is a root of $x^2+x+1$ mod $13$, i.e. $2^k\equiv3$ or $9$. As $2$ is a primitive root mod $13$ with $2^4\equiv3$, this means $k\equiv4,8\pmod{12}$. Fibonacci numbers mod $12$ show $F_{m-1}\equiv4$ or $8$ iff $m\equiv7\pmod{12}$. The $101$st smallest is $7+12\cdot100=1207$.

**Answer: 1207**

chmmc-2017-individual-15.title: Check
chmmc-2017-individual-15.body:
Computing $a_m$ exactly for $m\le29$ gives lucky $m=7,19$; evaluating $4^k+2^k+1$ mod $13$ with $k=F_{m-1}\bmod12$ for all $m<1300$ gives $7,19,31,\dots$ with the $101$st equal to $1207$.

**Answer: 1207**
